html:
An Inca stone estate high on a mountain ridge in southern Peru, built around 1450 for the emperor Pachacuti. It sits about 2,430 metres up, above the Urubamba River, a few days' walk from Cusco.

It was a royal retreat with temples, houses, baths and farming terraces. Its finest walls are cut stone fitted so closely that no mortar was needed. The Temple of the Sun and the carved stone called the Intihuatana probably marked the sun's movements.

The site was left empty around the time of the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire and the Spanish never found it, so it was not looted or destroyed. Local farmers knew it, but it became famous in 1911 when the American explorer Hiram Bingham brought it to the world's attention.

It became a World Heritage Site in 1983 and is now Peru's most visited place. Many visitors arrive on foot along a stretch of the Inca road known as the Inca Trail.
